title: Home or office? The impact of home and office attributes on workplace decisions in hybrid working

findings.antecedent: RPML model
findings.mechanism: capturing unobserved heterogeneity in preferences across individuals
findings.quote: the RPML model predicts choice behaviour better by accounting for heterogeneity.

findings.antecedent: 'no preference' option
findings.mechanism: workplace options were clearly defined and that the experimental setup effectively encouraged participants to make specific choices rather than opting out.
findings.quote: The utility of choosing 'no preference' was negative (βn=-6.168), suggesting that the workplace options were clearly defined

findings.antecedent: presence of direct colleagues at office
findings.mechanism: fosters interaction and collaboration
findings.quote: Direct colleagues in the office environment had a significant positive mean part-worth utility value (βdirect-colleagues=+0.697)

findings.antecedent: presence of direct colleagues at office
findings.mechanism: while direct colleagues encouraged the majority to be more likely to choose the office-workplace, a relatively small number of participants had negative preferences for it.
findings.quote: A significant standard deviation of 0.697 was observed for sharing the office with direct colleagues

findings.antecedent: presence of others (non-direct colleagues) at office
findings.mechanism: implied lack of specific interaction benefits compared to direct colleagues
findings.quote: indicating that participants preferred the office-workplace more when direct colleagues were present than when others (non-direct colleagues) were present.

findings.antecedent: no events at office
findings.mechanism: lack of engaging activities and interactions
findings.quote: Participants were less likely to prefer the office-workplace when no-events (βno-events = -0.458) were held at the office.

findings.antecedent: no events at office
findings.mechanism: while no-events reduced the appeal of the office-workplace for most participants, a small number of participants were less affected by this attribute in their decision.
findings.quote: However, significant variations were observed for this preference among participants (σno-events = 0.316)

findings.antecedent: social events at office
findings.mechanism: foster social interactions among colleagues
findings.quote: Participants preferred the office-workplace more when social events (βsocial = + 0.247) or wellness events (βwellness = + 0.211) were presented

findings.antecedent: wellness events at office
findings.mechanism: support breakout moments and foster social interactions
findings.quote: Participants preferred the office-workplace more when social events (βsocial = + 0.247) or wellness events (βwellness = + 0.211) were presented

findings.antecedent: kitchenette-only option at office
findings.mechanism: lack of engaging amenities
findings.quote: An office with a kitchenette-only option (βonly-kitch. = -0.340) discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace.

findings.antecedent: kitchenette with sitting area at office
findings.mechanism: support breakout moments and foster social interactions
findings.quote: In contrast, a kitchenette with a sitting area (βsitting = + 0.168) and with a sitting & gaming area (βsitting&gaming = + 0.172) encouraged participants to choose the office-workplace.

findings.antecedent: kitchenette with sitting and gaming area at office
findings.mechanism: support breakout moments and foster social interactions
findings.quote: In contrast, a kitchenette with a sitting area (βsitting = + 0.168) and with a sitting & gaming area (βsitting&gaming = + 0.172) encouraged participants to choose the office-workplace.

findings.antecedent: kitchenette with standing tables at office
findings.quote: However, a kitchenette with standing tables (βstanding tables = +0.000) did not have any influence on choice decisions.

findings.antecedent: smart technology at office
findings.mechanism: enhance work experiences
findings.quote: Smart technology (βsmart tech. = +0.163) enhanced the appeal of the office-workplace over the home-workplace for all participants

findings.antecedent: basic/regular technology at office
findings.mechanism: lack of enhanced work experiences
findings.quote: On the other hand, basic technology (βbasic tech. = -0.163) discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace.

findings.antecedent: single-office with non-transparent walls
findings.quote: For single offices with solid-walls, the mean utility was around zero (βsingle-solid walls = + 0.004), suggesting no impact on choice decisions

findings.antecedent: single-office with non-transparent walls
findings.mechanism: roughly half of the participants preferred this type of office, while the other half did not.
findings.quote: the significant standard deviation (σsingle-solid walls=1.024) indicates that roughly half of the participants preferred this type of office, while the other half did not.

findings.antecedent: single-office with one glass wall
findings.mechanism: provides a sense of openness while maintaining some privacy
findings.quote: In contrast, single offices with a glass-wall (βsingle-glass-wall = + 0.169) encouraged the majority of participants to prefer the office-workplace

findings.antecedent: single-office with one glass wall
findings.mechanism: considerable variation in preferences for this office type
findings.quote: though the standard deviation (σsingle-glass-wall=0.679) is rather large, meaning considerable variation in preferences for this office type.

findings.antecedent: open-office with half-wall separation
findings.mechanism: implied lack of privacy or noise distractions
findings.quote: Both kinds of open-offices, with half-walls (βopen-half-walls = -0.088) and with no-separation (βopen-no sepr = -0.085), somewhat discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace.

findings.antecedent: open-office with no separation
findings.mechanism: implied lack of privacy or noise distractions
findings.quote: Both kinds of open-offices, with half-walls (βopen-half-walls = -0.088) and with no-separation (βopen-no sepr = -0.085), somewhat discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace.

findings.antecedent: reservation required for office workspace
findings.mechanism: reduces flexibility of using spaces
findings.quote: If a reservation is required for a workseat (βrequired = -0.068), it discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace

findings.antecedent: reservation required for office workspace
findings.mechanism: while most had a negative preference for the requirement to reserve a workspace in advance, a considerable number of participants had less negative or positive preferences for this attribute
findings.quote: However, the significant standard deviation (σrequired = 0.268) indicates that while most had a negative preference for the requirement to reserve a workspace in advance, a considerable number of participants had less negative or positive preferences for this attribute

findings.antecedent: reservation not possible for office workspace
findings.mechanism: offers flexibility of using spaces without prior booking
findings.quote: If a reservation is required for a workseat (βrequired = -0.068), it discouraged participants from choosing the office-workplace over the home alternative.

findings.antecedent: warm colours, presence of plants and art objects at office
findings.quote: Lastly, aesthetics at the office-workplace showed no significant impact on choice behaviour with both levels

findings.antecedent: cool colours, no plants, no art objects at office
findings.quote: Lastly, aesthetics at the office-workplace showed no significant impact on choice behaviour with both levels

findings.antecedent: home-workplace (average home-attribute levels)
findings.consequent: base preference for choosing home-workplace over office-workplace
findings.mechanism: comfort and well-being perceived significantly higher at home
findings.quote: participants primarily had a base preference for choosing the home-workplace (βh=+0.863) over the office-workplace alternative.

findings.antecedent: home-workplace (average home-attribute levels)
findings.consequent: heterogeneity in base preference for home-workplace
findings.mechanism: while most participants had a base preference for the home-workplace, a notable proportion of participants had a base preference for the office-workplace.
findings.quote: However, the standard deviation (σh=1.346) showed a significant variation among participants for this base preference

findings.antecedent: commuting time between home and office < 15 min
findings.mechanism: shorter commutes make the office more appealing
findings.quote: A commuting time of less than 15 min (β<15min = -0.735) most strongly reduced the attractiveness of the home alternative

findings.antecedent: commuting time between home and office 15-30 min
findings.mechanism: shorter commutes make the office more appealing
findings.quote: followed by a commute time of between 15 and 30 min (β15-30 min = -0.395), which also reduced the appeal of the home alternative.

findings.antecedent: commuting time between home and office 15-30 min
findings.mechanism: while it discouraged most participants from choosing the home-workplace, it also led to a small proportion of participants with an increased preference for it.
findings.quote: A significant variation in preferences for commuting between 15 and 30 min among participants is observed (σ15-30 min = 0.554)

findings.antecedent: commuting time between home and office 30-45 min
findings.mechanism: longer commutes make working from home more appealing
findings.quote: Furthermore, a commuting time of between 30 and 45 min (β30-45 min = + 0.274) generally increased the appeal of the home-workplace

findings.antecedent: commuting time between home and office 30-45 min
findings.mechanism: considerable variation in preferences for this commuting time
findings.quote: σ30-45 = 0.747) generally increased the appeal of the home-workplace for most participants.

findings.antecedent: commuting time between home and office > 45 min
findings.mechanism: longer commutes make working from home more appealing
findings.quote: A commuting time of more than 45 min (β>45 min = + 0.856) had an even greater influence on encouraging participants to choose the home-workplace

findings.antecedent: having an ergonomic workstation at home
findings.mechanism: improves comfort and productivity
findings.quote: An ergonomic workstation at home (βergonomic = + 0.414) made participants more likely to choose the home-workplace

findings.antecedent: not having an ergonomic workstation at home
findings.mechanism: leads to physical discomfort and stress
findings.quote: An ergonomic workstation at home (βergonomic = + 0.414) made participants more likely to choose the home-workplace, and this preference was consistent across all participants.

findings.antecedent: having a dedicated workroom at home
findings.mechanism: supports comfort and productivity by providing a separate space for work
findings.quote: Participants were more likely to choose the home-workplace when they had a dedicated workroom (βa workroom = + 0.334) at home.

findings.antecedent: having a dedicated workroom at home
findings.mechanism: while most participants showed a positive preference for a dedicated workroom, for others, this preference was weaker or even negative.
findings.quote: However, the degree of this impact significantly varied among individuals (σa workroom = 1.687)

findings.antecedent: having a dedicated work area (but not a separate room) at home
findings.quote: The mean value of a dedicated work area (but not a separate room) was around zero

findings.antecedent: having a dedicated work area (but not a separate room) at home
findings.mechanism: for half of the participants, a dedicated work area made the home alternative more appealing, while for the other half, it did not.
findings.quote: with a significant standard deviation of 1.298. This means that for half of the participants, a dedicated work area made the home alternative more appealing, while for the other half, it did not.

findings.antecedent: having a non-specific home location (e.g., dining table) for work
findings.mechanism: lack of dedicated space for work
findings.quote: Participants were less likely to choose the home-workplace when they had a non-specific home location (βnon-specific = -0.323), such as a dining table.

findings.antecedent: others present at home during workday
findings.mechanism: can cause discomfort or distractions
findings.quote: most participants were less likely to choose the home-workplace when others (βothers present = -0.301) were present at home.

findings.antecedent: others present at home during workday
findings.mechanism: while most participants were less likely to choose the home alternative when others were present, a notable number of participants were more likely to choose the home alternative in the same situation.
findings.quote: However, a significant standard deviation (σothers present=0.606) indicated the variability in this preference.

findings.antecedent: no others present at home during workday
findings.mechanism: reduces distractions and increases privacy
findings.quote: most participants were less likely to choose the home-workplace when others (βothers present = -0.301) were present at home.

findings.antecedent: living in an apartment
findings.mechanism: implied limitations in space or privacy compared to other dwelling types
findings.quote: The impact of the type of dwelling varied, as indicated by the significant standard deviations, suggesting a wide range of preference differences among participants for working from home in an apartment

findings.antecedent: living in an apartment
findings.mechanism: Approximately half of the participants showed a negative preference for the apartment, semi-detached, or row-houses, while others showed the opposite.
findings.quote: significant standard deviations, suggesting a wide range of preference differences among participants for working from home in an apartment (σapartment = 1.053)

findings.antecedent: living in a semi-detached or row house
findings.mechanism: implied limitations in space or privacy compared to detached houses
findings.quote: The part worth utility for a detached house was 0.175 (βdetached house), suggesting that participants were more likely to work at home when they had their home-workplace in a detached house.

findings.antecedent: living in a semi-detached or row house
findings.mechanism: Approximately half of the participants showed a negative preference for the apartment, semi-detached, or row-houses, while others showed the opposite.
findings.quote: or semi-detached or row house (σsemi-detached, row = 1.041). Approximately half of the participants showed a negative preference for the apartment, semi-detached, or row-houses, while others showed the opposite.

findings.antecedent: living in a detached house
findings.mechanism: offers more space and privacy
findings.quote: The part worth utility for a detached house was 0.175 (βdetached house), suggesting that participants were more likely to work at home when they had their home-workplace in a detached house.

findings.antecedent: smart technology at home (employer supplied)
findings.mechanism: supports productivity and reduces communication barriers
findings.quote: Lastly, technology type impacted choice decisions, with smart technology showing a significant positive utility value (βsmart tech. = + 0.131)

findings.antecedent: basic/regular technology at home
findings.mechanism: lack of support for productivity and communication
findings.quote: Lastly, technology type impacted choice decisions, with smart technology showing a significant positive utility value (βsmart tech. = + 0.131) and no significant variations among participants, meaning that smart technology made the home-workplace more appealing for all participants.

stimuli.description: Two rendered images showcasing kitchenette and workspace with aesthetic elements (warm/cool colors, plants, art objects).

Text descriptions for 7 office attributes (workspace type, workspace access, aesthetics, technology level, other occupants, kitchenette, events) and 2 home attributes (technology level, presence of others), presented in 16 orthogonal fractional factorial combinations for office, plus participants' existing home setup.

tables.description: Categorization of workplace attributes into three environmental zones (Personal, Social, Public space) based on Hall's proxemics concept, with examples for office and home.

Lists 9 attributes (7 office, 2 home) and their levels that were systematically varied in the discrete choice experiment, categorized by environmental zones (E1, E2, E3) and linked to relevant literature.
Lists 4 individual-based home workplace attributes and their levels, collected via survey, categorized by environmental zones (E1, E2, E3) and linked to relevant literature.
Demographic characteristics (municipality, gender, age) and existing home-situation attributes (workstation type, workspace type, type of dwelling, commuting time) of the 1812 participants.
Correlation matrix showing the Spearman's rank correlation coefficients between the four individual-based home-situation attributes.
key_stats: All correlations were sufficiently low to include the individual-based attributes in the DCE model.

tables.description: Self-reported data on participants' office-dependency for work tasks (e.g., 'I can do all my work tasks remotely').
Multinomial Logit (MNL) and Random Parameter Mixed Logit (RPML) model results, showing mean part-worth utility (β) and standard deviation (σ) for each attribute level, along with significance levels.

limitations: The sample includes employees from three cities of different scales, Amsterdam, Almere, and Eindhoven, each with distinct dwelling types, which may further contribute to these variations in preferences.
This study focused on civil servants working in municipal office buildings, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings to other types of office workers.
The findings are based on hypothetical scenarios presented in the discrete choice experiment, which may not fully capture the complexities of real-world office environments.
Participants may have evaluated familiar office attributes more reliably than unfamiliar ones.

Although this study explicitly asked participants to assume no home obligations (e.g., childcare, package delivery, shopping), such responsibilities may nonetheless influence real-world workplace choices.
Although this study revealed heterogeneity in workplace preferences, it did not examine personal characteristics such as gender, age, or education level.

This study examined three environmental zones with a total of only eleven home and office attributes. Future studies should build on the findings of this study and explore additional attributes to provide further understanding of workplace preferences within these three environment zones.

Aesthetics were assessed by combining three elements (colour, presence of art and greenery). However, each of these elements may impact office attractiveness in different ways. Future hybrid studies should therefore investigate them separately to understand how either combinations or separate effects influence the office's appeal.
